Frequently Asked Questions

Everything you need to know about cats

Cats purr for many reasons — contentment, self-soothing, and healing. Purring is a complex behavior triggered by emotions and physical states. Mother cats purr to guide kittens, while adult cats purr when relaxed or seeking attention. Interestingly, cats also purr when injured or stressed, suggesting it may have evolved as a self-healing mechanism.

Cats are champion sleepers, spending 12-16 hours per day sleeping or in a resting state. This is a remnant of their wild ancestry — in the wild, cats conserve energy through extended sleep, allowing them to hunt during peak activity times. Kittens and senior cats may sleep even more, up to 20 hours daily.

Cats have a wide range of vocalizations, each with its own meaning. Short meows are greetings, long meows express complaints or demands, and rapid-fire meows show excitement. Chirps and trills indicate friendly communication, while hisses and growls are clear warnings. Interestingly, cats rarely meow at each other — they reserve this behavior mainly for communicating with humans.

The third eyelid, called the nictitating membrane, is a protective covering that helps keep a cat's eyes moist and clean. It sweeps across the eye to remove debris and protective secretions. If a cat's third eyelid becomes visible, it can be a sign of illness or stress, so it's worth consulting a veterinarian if you notice this change.

Cats possess an incredible righting reflex that allows them to rotate their bodies mid-air to land on their feet. This ability relies on their flexible spine, keen inner ear balance system, and visual processing. Starting from just a few feet, kittens gradually develop this skill, which becomes nearly automatic by adulthood. However, falls from extreme heights can still cause serious injury.

Cats have superior night vision compared to humans, thanks to a high concentration of rod cells in their retinas and a reflective layer called the tapetum lucidum. This layer acts like a mirror, bouncing light back through the retina to increase sensitivity. While cats can't see in complete darkness, they need only about one-sixth the light that humans require to see clearly.

Cats are incredibly athletic and can jump up to six times their body length horizontally and eight times their body length vertically. This remarkable jumping ability comes from their powerful hind legs, flexible spine, and excellent depth perception. A typical cat can leap onto a 6-foot fence with ease, making them impressive acrobats in the animal world.

Cats knock things off surfaces for several reasons: curiosity about how objects behave, testing their hunting and pouncing skills, or seeking attention from their owners. Some behavioral experts believe it's also a way for cats to mark territory or create an enriched environment. While frustrating for humans, this behavior is completely normal feline activity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Everything you need to know about cats

Cats purr for many reasons — contentment, self-soothing, and healing. Purring is a complex behavior triggered by emotions and physical states. Mother cats purr to guide kittens, while adult cats purr when relaxed or seeking attention. Interestingly, cats also purr when injured or stressed, suggesting it may have evolved as a self-healing mechanism.

Cats are champion sleepers, spending 12-16 hours per day sleeping or in a resting state. This is a remnant of their wild ancestry — in the wild, cats conserve energy through extended sleep, allowing them to hunt during peak activity times. Kittens and senior cats may sleep even more, up to 20 hours daily.

Cats have a wide range of vocalizations, each with its own meaning. Short meows are greetings, long meows express complaints or demands, and rapid-fire meows show excitement. Chirps and trills indicate friendly communication, while hisses and growls are clear warnings. Interestingly, cats rarely meow at each other — they reserve this behavior mainly for communicating with humans.

The third eyelid, called the nictitating membrane, is a protective covering that helps keep a cat's eyes moist and clean. It sweeps across the eye to remove debris and protective secretions. If a cat's third eyelid becomes visible, it can be a sign of illness or stress, so it's worth consulting a veterinarian if you notice this change.

Cats possess an incredible righting reflex that allows them to rotate their bodies mid-air to land on their feet. This ability relies on their flexible spine, keen inner ear balance system, and visual processing. Starting from just a few feet, kittens gradually develop this skill, which becomes nearly automatic by adulthood. However, falls from extreme heights can still cause serious injury.

Cats have superior night vision compared to humans, thanks to a high concentration of rod cells in their retinas and a reflective layer called the tapetum lucidum. This layer acts like a mirror, bouncing light back through the retina to increase sensitivity. While cats can't see in complete darkness, they need only about one-sixth the light that humans require to see clearly.

Cats are incredibly athletic and can jump up to six times their body length horizontally and eight times their body length vertically. This remarkable jumping ability comes from their powerful hind legs, flexible spine, and excellent depth perception. A typical cat can leap onto a 6-foot fence with ease, making them impressive acrobats in the animal world.

Cats knock things off surfaces for several reasons: curiosity about how objects behave, testing their hunting and pouncing skills, or seeking attention from their owners. Some behavioral experts believe it's also a way for cats to mark territory or create an enriched environment. While frustrating for humans, this behavior is completely normal feline activity.
